about.title: Norco Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Norco's economy runs on a blend of equestrian facilities, small industrial operations, warehousing near I-15, and family-owned businesses along 6th Street and River Road. Workers in these settings face real risks - from equipment malfunctions to falls to vehicle collisions on the job. Under California law, workers' compensation is typically your only path against your employer, no matter who caused the accident, but if a subcontractor, equipment manufacturer, property owner, or another driver contributed to your injury, you may have a separate third-party claim worth pursuing. Riverside County workplaces vary widely, and figuring out whether a third party bears responsibility can be complicated without help. LawProactive doesn't practice law - we connect injured workers in Norco with an independent attorney who can review the facts, explain your options honestly, and pursue a third-party claim if one exists, all while you focus on healing.

items.question: I was hurt at work in Norco - can I sue my employer directly?
items.answer: In most cases, California workers' compensation is your exclusive remedy against your employer, regardless of fault. However, if a third party like a subcontractor, property owner, or equipment manufacturer contributed to your injury, you may be able to file a separate claim against them. An independent attorney can help you sort out which path applies to your situation.

items.question: Does it matter that my injury happened near Hamner Avenue or I-15?
items.answer: Location itself doesn't change your legal rights, but if your injury involved a vehicle collision while working near these corridors, it could open the door to a third-party claim against another driver. Norco's mix of equestrian, industrial, and commuter traffic on routes like Hamner and I-15 means these situations come up more than people expect. An attorney can review the specifics with you.

items.question: How long do I have to report my injury or file a claim?
items.answer: You generally need to report a workplace injury to your employer within 30 days to protect your workers' comp rights. If a third party is involved, California law gives you 2 years from the date of injury to file that separate claim. Missing either deadline can limit your options, so it helps to get guidance early.
